title: How do you brainstorm ideas with structure in a case interview?
description: "What could the client do?" is still a structuring question. Use buckets, not a list.
hook: "What else could the client do?" sounds like an invitation to list every idea in your head. Interviewers are actually looking for something more organised: ideas grouped into buckets so nothing big is missed. This guide shows you how to brainstorm with structure, even when you are put on the spot.
body:
In this guide

  • Never list randomly
  • Add one real-world example
  • Prioritise before you stop
  • A worked example
  • What to remember
  • Check yourself

Never list randomly

When asked "what could explain this?" or "how could they fix it?", take ten seconds and answer as a mini-tree. Two or three buckets are enough: internal vs external, short-term vs long-term, revenue vs cost, customers vs company vs competitors. Then give 2-3 ideas under each.

Add one real-world example

One concrete example from a real company lifts an answer from "good" to "memorable": for a question about raising revenue per customer, "Airlines did this by charging separately for bags and seat choice." Use at most one or two per case, as seasoning. Keep an idea or two in reserve, because the interviewer will often ask "anything else?"

Prioritise before you stop

End by saying which idea you'd pursue first and why, usually based on impact, cost and speed. A list without a priority leaves the interviewer to do your job.

See it in action: How could a coffee chain make delivery more profitable?

"I'd think about it in two buckets: making each delivery order more profitable, and moving customers to cheaper channels. On the first: raise app menu prices, as many chains do; negotiate the commission down for volume; build a delivery menu around high-margin items. On the second: a click-and-collect option in our own app, with loyalty points to make the switch worth it. I'd start with app pricing, because it's fast and needs no investment."

What to remember

  • Two or three buckets, then ideas under each.
  • One real example, used sparingly.
  • Finish with a priority.

Check yourself

Have a go at each one before you open the answer. Getting some wrong is how it sticks.

1. Which opening is strongest for a brainstorm?

  • "Lots of things could help, for example..."
  • "I’d think about this in two buckets: internal and external."
  • "Let me list every idea I can think of."
Show the answer

"I’d think about this in two buckets: internal and external.". Buckets show structure and make your ideas easy to follow.

Try it now

A UK university wants to attract more international students. Give your ideas in 2-3 buckets, then pick one to start with.

Give yourself 2 minutes, out loud if you can. Speaking it, rather than thinking it, is what builds the skill.

Show a strong answer

Attract: scholarships in priority countries, partnerships with schools abroad, better rankings visibility. Convert: faster offers, visa and accommodation support, alumni calls with applicants. Access: joint programmes and online pathway courses. Start with conversion: it’s fast and works on students who already applied.
outro: You do not have to get all of this right at once. Pick one thing from this guide to focus on in your next practice case. This guide is lesson 8 of the free PrepForCase course, where you can do the exercise and quiz and track your progress.
